title: Why the Sons of Sceva Thought Power Could Be Borrowed
paragraphs:
Why the Sons of Sceva Thought Power Could Be Borrowed
They Used the Name of Jesus Like a Tool… Until the Demons Answered Back
Some stories in Scripture are so shocking that they feel almost uncomfortable to read.
Because hidden inside a strange encounter with demons, public humiliation, and seven terrified brothers running naked through the streets is a warning that still confronts the modern Church.
And the devastating difference between knowing about Jesus and actually belonging to Him.

The story unfolds in Ephesus, a city overflowing with spiritual confusion. Magic was normal. Occult practices were common. People chased power through rituals, incantations, secret names, and mystical formulas. In a culture obsessed with supernatural control, many believed power could be accessed if you simply learned the right words.
Through the preaching of Paul, lives were transformed. Miracles occurred. Demonic oppression was broken. The Gospel spread with undeniable force.
Especially the sons of a Jewish chief priest named Sceva.
“Then certain of the vagabond Jews, exorcists, took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, ‘We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth.’” (Acts 19:13)
The Greek text uses the phrase:

ὁρκίζω ὑμᾶς τὸν Ἰησοῦν
(horkizō hymas ton Iēsoun)
“I command you under oath by Jesus.”
They were not surrendering to Jesus.
They were attempting to use Jesus.
To them, the name of Christ was not a Savior to worship.
It was a formula to exploit.
And before we judge them too quickly, we should ask ourselves an uncomfortable question.
How many people today approach Jesus the same way?
Some want His blessings without repentance.
The sons of Sceva believed authority could be borrowed because they misunderstood where spiritual authority originates.
In Scripture, authority is never detached from relationship.
When Jesus sent out His disciples, authority flowed from union with Him.
When the apostles cast out demons, authority flowed from submission to Him.
When believers prayed, authority flowed from belonging to Him.
The Hebrew worldview never separated power from covenant relationship.
Throughout the Old Testament, God's people understood this deeply.
The Hebrew word for knowing someone is יָדַע (yada').
It means far more than intellectual awareness.
The sons of Sceva knew the name.
But they did not know the Person.
Then comes one of the most terrifying moments in the entire New Testament.
“And the evil spirit answered and said, ‘Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye?’”
Τὸν Ἰησοῦν γινώσκω, καὶ τὸν Παῦλον ἐπίσταμαι· ὑμεῖς δὲ τίνες ἐστέ;
(Ton Iēsoun ginōskō, kai ton Paulon epistamai; hymeis de tines este?)
But the seven men possess no spiritual identity.
They attempted to wield a sword they had never been given.
“And the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, and overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.” (Acts 19:16)
Everything they thought they possessed vanished in a single moment.
And suddenly the story becomes deeply personal.
Because exposure is often God's mercy.
Many people spend years constructing religious appearances.
Yet beneath the surface there is no genuine surrender.
And what was merely borrowed cannot survive the storm.
Only what is genuinely rooted in Christ remains.
The sons of Sceva wanted power.
That is still the great divide today.
Jesus never invited people into a system of religious performance.
The Greek word often translated “abide” is:
“Abide in me, and I in you.” (John 15:4)
Everything changes when authority flows from intimacy rather than imitation.
The aftermath of the sons of Sceva's failure reveals something extraordinary.
People realized Jesus was not a magical formula.
“And the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified.”
They burned their expensive magic books.
The scandal became a doorway to grace.
And isn't that exactly what Jesus does?
A murderer named Moses becomes a deliverer.
An adulterer named David becomes a man after God's own heart.
A denier named Peter becomes a pillar of the Church.
A persecutor named Saul becomes the Apostle Paul.
And seven humiliated brothers become a warning that still points people toward genuine faith two thousand years later.
Because Jesus specializes in rewriting stories.
That is why the Gospel remains the greatest story ever told.
Maybe as you read this, you recognize something of yourself in the sons of Sceva.
Maybe you've been borrowing someone else's faith.
Maybe you've known about Jesus for years without truly knowing Him.
The Gospel is not an invitation to perform.
It is an invitation to surrender.
The Son of God entered human history, lived the sinless life we could never live, died for our sins upon the cross, and rose again victorious over death.
The power of Christ was never meant to be borrowed.
And that transformation begins when a sinner stops reaching for power and starts reaching for Jesus.
Be honest. This may have hit harder than you expected.
Someone you know is trying to survive on borrowed faith right now.

If this ministry has encouraged you, strengthened your faith, or helped you understand Scripture more clearly, supporting it is one practical way to participate in spreading the Gospel and glorifying God through the stewardship of resources He has entrusted to us.
Because one day every borrowed thing will be stripped away, and only what was built through a real relationship with Jesus Christ will remain.
